sattapaṇṇiguhā.notes: DN 16 places the cave on the slope of Vebhāra at Rājagaha. The SN 1.20 citation leads to Samiddhi at the hot springs and gives no evidence for the cave or the council.

sañjaya.notes: DN 2, DN 16, MN 30, SN 3.1, SN 44.9 and Snp 3.6 also name Belaṭṭhaputta, using the spelling Sañcaya. DPD gives those forms a separate lemma, sañcaya 2.1. DN 1 discusses the doctrine, and the AN 5 citations concern classes of people. Neither names the teacher. The elder signs Thag 1.48, verse 48. The TH50 hint needs checking.

sañjīva.notes: MN 50 tells how the woodcutters mistook the meditating disciple for dead. DN 14:1.9.4 and SN 15.20:2.8 also pair him with Vidhura in the compound vidhurasañjīvaṁ, which has its own dictionary line. The packet has no entry for the hell.

saṅgārava.notes: AN 5.193 and SN 46.55 contain the question about remembering hymns. The entry also covers the student at Caṇḍalakappa in MN 100 and the ritual bather at Sāvatthī in SN 7.21, and questions whether these are the same brahmin. AN 3.59, MN 99, SN 7.19–20 and SN 46.54 are neighboring texts. The hits in AN 5.200, AN 10.122, SN 7.22 and SN 46.56 are chapter summaries.

saṅkha.notes: DN 26 identifies the future king of Ketumatī. The entry describes Mahāpanāda’s palace as a gift to the Saṅgha. DN 26:26.1–2 calls it a yūpa (sacrificial post) and includes ascetics, brahmins and the poor among the recipients of Saṅkha’s gifts.

saṅkicca.notes: MN 36, MN 76 and AN 6.57 name the ascetic Kisa Saṅkicca alongside Nanda Vaccha and Makkhali Gosāla. Thag 11.1 attributes its verses to the elder Saṅkicca. Only the elder has a candidate entry, so attaching it to the DPD line for Kisa would misidentify the ascetic.

sela.notes: MN 92:6.2 and Snp 3.7:6.2 give Sela 300 students. The entry says 250 accompanied him. Thag 16.6 preserves his verses. MN 91 and MN 93 are neighboring discourses. The packet hits in SN 5.9 and Thig 3.7 belong to the nun Selā.

selā.notes: Thig 3.7 names Selā and preserves the temptation to enjoy sensual pleasures. SN 5.1 gives parallel verses under Āḷavikā, the name DPPN also gives her. In the cited SN 5.9 Māra asks Selā who made the puppet. SN 5.8 concerns Sīsupacālā, and SN 5.10 concerns Vajirā with Selā only in its chapter summary. MN 92, Snp 3.7 and Thag 16.6 name the male Sela.

seniya.notes: MN 57 identifies Seniya as the naked dog-votary. Every other listed discourse uses Seniya for King Bimbisāra of Magadha. MN 56 is a neighboring citation.

serī.notes: SN 2.23 names the godling Serī. In his account of his former gifts, SN 2.23:8.1 spells his name as king Sirī. SN 2.21 and SN 2.22 name the godlings Siva and Khema respectively. Serī also appears in the chapter summary at SN 2.30:18.1.

seta.notes: SN 2.30:16.3 names the Himalayan peak. SN 3.1 is a neighboring citation. AN 6.43:3.1 explicitly calls Pasenadi’s elephant seto nāma nāgo. Sujato translates the name as ‘White’, so the packet misses the elephant’s sutta.

sikhāmoggallāna.notes: The brahmin reports Soṇakāyana’s claim about deeds in AN 4.234. AN 4.233 is a neighboring citation.

sikhī.notes: DN 14 and SN 12.5 identify the fully awakened Buddha. MN 116:6.26 names a separate Sikhī among the independent Buddhas, for whom there is no candidate. Of SN 12.4–10 only SN 12.5 is his discourse, with another mention in the chapter summary at SN 12.10:8.2. Thag 7.5:4.2 names him with Vessabhū, but the English names fall in the following segment.

sirivaḍḍha.notes: SN 47.30 concerns the householder Mānadinna. Its closing list names Sirivaḍḍha as the title of the preceding discourse, SN 47.29. There Ānanda confirms the householder’s report that he has abandoned the five lower fetters. MN 87 and SN 47.28 are neighboring citations.

siva.notes: Despite the empty mention list, SN 2.21:1.3 names the visiting godling sivo devaputto. Sujato spells his name ‘Shiva’. SN 2.20 is about Anāthapiṇḍika. Siva also occurs in the chapter summary at SN 2.30:18.1.

sobhita.notes: DPD and DPPN both read sobhito in the list of independent Buddhas at MN 116:6.35 as a name. Sujato reads it as ‘beautiful’, describing Mānatthaddha. This accounts for the sense match and the missing packet mention. MN 117 is a neighboring citation. AN 1.227 and Thag 2.23 identify the elder through his recollection of past lives. The two following AN groups add no instance. Neither entry describes the earlier fully awakened Buddha.

somā.notes: MN 90 names Somā and Sakulā as sisters and has Pasenadi convey their greeting. It leaves their marital status unstated. SN 5.2 and Thig 3.8 share the exchange on women’s wisdom. DN 13 invokes the male deity Soma. The English of AN 8.91–117 includes a laywoman Somā, but the local Pāli list passes from Khemā to Rucī and the English gives no link to Sakulā. AN 8.89–90, MN 89, SN 5.1 and SN 5.3 are neighboring citations. SN 5.10:8.1 also lists the nun in the chapter summary.

sovīra.notes: DN 19:36.6 pairs the Sovīras with Roruka. DPD locates the country in the lower Indus valley. DPPN also reports a proposed location in Gujarat. The verse gives the capital but does not settle the modern location.

soṇa.notes: The harp-strings lesson in the Cool Grove (AN 6.55) identifies DPD’s generic monk as Koḷivisa, so both lines take Soṇa 05. AN 1.205 names Koḷivisa and AN 1.206 names Kuṭikaṇṇa, making a single pick for AN 1.198–208 impossible. DN 14:1.9.3 pairs Vessabhū’s disciple Soṇa with Uttara in the compound soṇuttaraṁ. Thag 2.37 names a further elder, Soṇa Poṭiriya, without a candidate. AN 1.241 and Thig 5.8 name the nun Soṇā, and AN 8.91–117 lists a laywoman Soṇā. The householder’s son appears in SN 22.49–50 and SN 35.128. DPD’s SN 22.44 hint and the page placements at SN 22.48, SN 35.127 and SN 35.129 miss him. AN 1.209–218 and AN 1.219–234 also miss the two foremost monks.
